Complete PLL phase-noise budget and optimal loop BW

Prerequisites: white_noise_to_phase_noise (where the VCO term Svco∝Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si/f2S_{vco}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i/f^2Svco​∝Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​/f2 comes from), serdes_clocking_connection (the CDR/PLL's high-pass on the VCO, jitter integration bandwidth), lc_vs_ring (why ring's SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ is high and LC's is low) | Next: exercises, lab_13_pll_cdr_transfer

This page answers a question a system-design engineer faces every day: for a phase-locked loop (PLL — a negative-feedback loop that locks an oscillator's phase to a reference clock), which sources contribute how much to the output phase noise, and which one dominates at which offset band? How wide should the loop bandwidth (the highest offset the feedback can still track) be chosen to minimize total jitter? We write out the transfer function of each of the five noise sources to the output, sum them as

Sout=(SrefN2+Scp) ∣Hlp∣2+Svco ∣Hhp∣2S_{out}=(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+S_{vco}\,\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2Sout​=(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2

(canonical Section 11.2, "PLL output noise budget"; for a fractional-N loop a third term — the ΔΣ quantization noise SΔΣ ∣Hlp∣2S_{\Delta\Sigma}\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2SΔΣ​∣Hlp​∣2 — must be added, see the section "The third term for fractional-N" on this page; it is zero for integer-N), then minimize ∫Sout df\int S_{out}\,df∫Sout​df (integrated phase variance, proportional to rms jitter squared) to find that famous U-shaped curve and its minimum.

Physical intuition (conclusion first): a PLL is a low-pass tracker. Within the loop bandwidth fnf_nfn​, the feedback reacts fast enough that the output follows the reference — so the noise of the reference and the loop's front end (PFD, charge-pump, divider) is amplified and low-passed onto the output (and the reference is also multiplied by NNN, so its power is multiplied by N2N^2N2); meanwhile the VCO's own close-in drift is corrected away by the feedback (VCO high-pass). Beyond fnf_nfn​, the feedback can't keep up, and the output follows the free-running VCO — the VCO's 1/f21/f^21/f2 noise leaks straight through. So in-band tracks ref/CP, out-of-band tracks VCO, with the crossover at fnf_nfn​. Set fnf_nfn​ too narrow → too much VCO leaks through (U-shape's left arm rises); too wide → too much ref/CP gets carried through (right arm rises). There must be an optimal fnf_nfn​ in between.

This page's PLL closed-loop transfer function (loop transfer / open-loop gain / type-II stability — the higher-order details) belongs to standard PLL literature (Gardner, Razavi, Best), not among the five source PDFs downloaded for this site; we only cite its type-II second-order closed-loop result (already recorded in canonical Section 10.2), and focus on "the ISF determines the VCO term SvcoS_{vco}Svco​" and "how the budget sums up and how the optimal BW is found." The microscopic origin of the VCO term (Γrms2/qmax2\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2Γrms2​/qmax2​) is precisely the output of this site's whole ISF theory built up so far.

Why do a "noise budget"​

Phase noise is not a single number — it's a curve that varies with offset, and different sources dominate different segments of that curve. Doing a budget = plotting each source as one curve, and seeing where each one pokes up and what the total looks like. The value of doing this:

  • Find the bottleneck: close-in too high? Usually the reference or the charge-pump (amplified by N2N^2N2). Far-out too high? It's the VCO. Treat the actual cause, don't swap parts blindly.
  • Choose the loop BW: the crossover point and total jitter are both strongly tied to fnf_nfn​; the budget lets you quantify this trade-off.
  • Connect to system metrics: integrate SoutS_{out}Sout​ to get rms jitter σt\sigma_tσt​, and feed it directly into the SerDes eye/BER (see serdes_clocking_connection).

PLL block diagram and the five noise sources​

The skeleton of an integer-N PLL: reference clock → phase detector (PFD, phase-frequency detector) + charge-pump (turns the phase error into current pulses) → loop filter (integrates the current into a control voltage) → VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) → divider (÷N, pulls the output back down to the reference frequency for comparison). The five noise injection points, shown below:

Each source takes a different path to the output, so the shaping differs:

SourceSymbolPhysical originTransfer to outputShaping at output
referenceSrefS_{ref}Sref​crystal/reference phase noise×N\times N×N then low-passN2∣Hlp∣2N^2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2N2∣Hlp​∣2 (in-band, amplified by N2N^2N2)
PFD/charge-pumpScpS_{cp}Scp​CP current noise, PFD dead-zone, mismatchlow-pass∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (in-band, flat floor)
dividerSdivS_{div}Sdiv​jitter of the ÷N logiclow-pass (same path as ref)∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (in-band; often folded into ScpS_{cp}Scp​)
loop filterSlfS_{lf}Slf​filter resistor thermal noise modulating the VCOband-pass (peaks near fnf_nfn​)∝∣Hlp∣2\propto\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∝∣Hlp​∣2 (usually small, omitted)
VCOSvcoS_{vco}Svco​tank/tail thermal noise via ISF (this site's main thread)high-pass∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hhp​∣2 (dominates out-of-band)

Why the reference is multiplied by N2N^2N2. The divider pulls the output frequency fout=Nfreff_{out}=N f_{ref}fout​=Nfref​ back down to freff_{ref}fref​ for comparison — equivalent to requiring output phase = N×N\timesN× reference phase (phase is also multiplied up). Phase amplified by NNN means power spectral density amplified by N2N^2N2. So a clean crystal (SrefS_{ref}Sref​ very low) combined with a large NNN (e.g. N=100N=100N=100) has its equivalent in-band noise floor at the output raised by 20log⁡10N=4020\log_{10}N=4020log10​N=40 dB — this is why an integer-N PLL's in-band noise is usually determined jointly by the reference ×N2\times N^2×N2 and the charge-pump, not the VCO.

Design takeaway: the in-band floor ≈(SrefN2+Scp)\approx(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})≈(Sref​N2+Scp​); to suppress it, either lower NNN (use fractional-N or a higher-frequency reference), or lower the charge-pump's current noise. The VCO contributes nothing in-band (it's corrected away by the high-pass).

Step 1: each source's transfer function (type-II second-order)​

Using the closed-loop power transfer of canonical Section 10.2, "PLL (type-II 2nd order)." With natural frequency ωn=2πfn\omega_n=2\pi f_nωn​=2πfn​, damping ratio ζ\zetaζ (this page uses near-critical ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707), and ω=2πf\omega=2\pi fω=2πf (fff the offset frequency):

∣Hlp∣2=(2ζωnω)2+ωn4(ωn2−ω2)2+(2ζωnω)2,∣Hhp∣2=ω4(ωn2−ω2)2+(2ζωnω)2.\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2=\frac{(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2+\omega_n^4}{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2},\qquad \lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2=\frac{\omega^4}{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2}.∣Hlp​∣2=(ωn2​−ω2)2+(2ζωn​ω)2(2ζωn​ω)2+ωn4​​,∣Hhp​∣2=(ωn2​−ω2)2+(2ζωn​ω)2ω4​.
  • Low-frequency limit ω→0\omega\to0ω→0: ∣Hlp∣2→ωn4/ωn4=1\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\to\omega_n^4/\omega_n^4=1∣Hlp​∣2→ωn4​/ωn4​=1 (reference/CP fully pass), ∣Hhp∣2→0\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\to0∣Hhp​∣2→0 (VCO suppressed). Confirms "in-band tracks ref/CP."
  • High-frequency limit ω→∞\omega\to\inftyω→∞: ∣Hlp∣2→(2ζωnω)2/ω4→0\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\to(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2/\omega^4\to0∣Hlp​∣2→(2ζωn​ω)2/ω4→0, ∣Hhp∣2→ω4/ω4=1\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\to\omega^4/\omega^4=1∣Hhp​∣2→ω4/ω4=1 (VCO fully passes). Confirms "out-of-band tracks VCO."
  • Complementarity: in the standard form Hhp(s)=1−Hlp(s)H_{hp}(s)=1-H_{lp}(s)Hhp​(s)=1−Hlp​(s), so the output is the sum of the two paths with no double-counting.
  • Dimension check: ω,ωn\omega,\omega_nω,ωn​ are both rad/s, numerator and denominator are the same order (ω4\omega^4ω4 or ωn4\omega_n^4ωn4​), ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2 is dimensionless — confirmed.

The detailed derivation of these two transfer functions (writing the open-loop gain G(s)=KdKvF(s)/sG(s)=K_dK_vF(s)/sG(s)=Kd​Kv​F(s)/s from the PFD gain KdK_dKd​, VCO gain KvK_vKv​, and loop filter F(s)F(s)F(s), then taking the closed loop) is in lab_13_pll_cdr_transfer; that derivation chain and type-II stability belong to standard PLL literature (not among the five source PDFs).

Step 2: summing into the output budget​

The reference and charge-pump/divider take the same low-pass path (with the reference first multiplied by NNN), the VCO takes the high-pass path, and the three segments are uncorrelated — their powers add (canonical Section 11.2):

Sout(f)=(Sref(f) N2+Scp(f)) ∣Hlp(f)∣2+Svco(f) ∣Hhp(f)∣2.S_{out}(f)=\big(S_{ref}(f)\,N^2+S_{cp}(f)\big)\,\lvert H_{lp}(f)\rvert^2+S_{vco}(f)\,\lvert H_{hp}(f)\rvert^2 .Sout​(f)=(Sref​(f)N2+Scp​(f))∣Hlp​(f)∣2+Svco​(f)∣Hhp​(f)∣2.
  • Dimension check: Sref,Scp,Svco,SoutS_{ref},S_{cp},S_{vco},S_{out}Sref​,Scp​,Svco​,Sout​ are all rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz, NNN and ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2 are dimensionless, so the three terms add in the same units — confirmed.
  • Where did the divider go: SdivS_{div}Sdiv​ takes the same low-pass path as the charge-pump and is shaped identically by ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 at the output, so in practice SdivS_{div}Sdiv​ is often folded into ScpS_{cp}Scp​ as "the loop front end's equivalent in-band floor." This page's ScpS_{cp}Scp​ is the combined total of "PFD + charge-pump + divider."
  • The loop-filter term: SlfS_{lf}Slf​'s (loop-filter resistor thermal noise modulating the VCO) transfer has a small peak near fnf_nfn​, usually smaller in magnitude than ref/CP and VCO; this page's toy budget omits it (marked illustrative). A real design needs to include it and optimize resistor noise.
  • The fractional-N third term: if the divider modulus is dithered by a ΔΣ modulator (fractional-N), the quantization noise enters the budget as SΔΣ(f) ∣Hlp∣2S_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2SΔΣ​(f)∣Hlp​∣2 — same low-pass path as the CP, but not multiplied by N2N^2N2, and shaped as a rising ramp of +20(m−1)+20(m-1)+20(m−1) dB/dec. Full derivation and worked example in the section "The third term for fractional-N: ΔΣ quantization noise" on this page. For integer-N (this page's lab_20 setup) this term is zero.

The VCO term is precisely this site's ISF result​

SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ doesn't come out of thin air — it is exactly the output of this site's whole ISF theory. In the 1/f21/f^21/f2 region (white-noise upconversion),

Svco(f)=Γrms2qmax2⋅in2‾/Δf(2πf)2[rad2/Hz]S_{vco}(f)=\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^2}{q_{max}^2}\cdot\frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{(2\pi f)^2}\quad[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]Svco​(f)=qmax2​Γrms2​​⋅(2πf)2in2​​/Δf​[rad2/Hz]

(clean time-domain version, see white_noise_to_phase_noise; corresponds to [P1] Eq.(21), p.185, off by an SSB factor-of-2). So the answer to "why is the VCO term 1/f21/f^21/f2 in the PLL budget, why ∝Γrms2/qmax2\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2∝Γrms2​/qmax2​" is entirely in the ISF. A ring VCO has a large Γrms\Gamma_{rms}Γrms​ and small qmaxq_{max}qmax​, so SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ is high (see lc_vs_ring) — this is exactly the root reason a ring-PLL needs to open up fnf_nfn​ to suppress the VCO.

Step 3: the in-band vs out-of-band handoff​

Break SoutS_{out}Sout​ into three segments:

  1. Deep in-band (f≪fnf\ll f_nf≪fn​): ∣Hlp∣2≈1\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1∣Hlp​∣2≈1, ∣Hhp∣2≈0\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\approx0∣Hhp​∣2≈0. Sout≈SrefN2+ScpS_{out}\approx S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}Sout​≈Sref​N2+Scp​ — a flat floor set by the reference×N2\times N^2×N2 and the charge-pump (if the reference contains 1/f1/f1/f, this segment tilts up slightly toward close-in).
  2. Out-of-band (f≫fnf\gg f_nf≫fn​): ∣Hlp∣2≈0\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx0∣Hlp​∣2≈0, ∣Hhp∣2≈1\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\approx1∣Hhp​∣2≈1. Sout≈Svco∝1/f2S_{out}\approx S_{vco}\propto1/f^2Sout​≈Svco​∝1/f2 — the VCO's −20-20−20 dB/decade skirt leaks straight through.
  3. Crossover (f≈fnf\approx f_nf≈fn​): the two segments meet. At ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707, at fnf_nfn​ ∣Hlp∣2≈1.5\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1.5∣Hlp​∣2≈1.5 (+1.76+1.76+1.76 dB), ∣Hhp∣2≈0.5\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\approx0.5∣Hhp​∣2≈0.5 (−3-3−3 dB), and their sum ≈2\approx2≈2 (+3+3+3 dB) — this is the slight peaking, also the origin of the common "bump near the loop BW" seen in PLL output (the two curves are actually equal at f≈1.55 fnf\approx1.55\,f_nf≈1.55fn​, each about 0.850.850.85, −0.7-0.7−0.7 dB, not at fnf_nfn​). Too small a ζ\zetaζ (underdamped) makes the peaking sharp. The exact location and height of the peak actually have a closed-form solution — see the next section.

Reading a PN plot at a glance: see a flat close-in floor → measure in-band, back out SrefN2+ScpS_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}Sref​N2+Scp​; see the floor start falling at −20-20−20 dB/dec from some offset → that knee is fnf_nfn​, beyond it is VCO. A sharp peak in the middle → insufficient damping or an overshooting loop-BW design.

Supplementary derivation: the closed-form peaking — a type-II with a zero is destined to bump​

Step 3 measured ∣Hlp∣2≈1.5\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1.5∣Hlp​∣2≈1.5 (+1.76+1.76+1.76 dB) at f=fnf=f_nf=fn​ — but that is not the maximum. This section solves analytically for the peak frequency and peak magnitude of the type-II second-order ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (the canonical Section-10.2 form). The derivation itself is pure algebra (self-contained); the "ζ↔\zeta\leftrightarrowζ↔ phase margin mapping" and the "cascaded 0.1-dB rule" belong to standard control/telecom literature, each labeled as such (external literature, not among this site's five source PDFs).

Normalization​

Let x=ω/ωn=f/fnx=\omega/\omega_n=f/f_nx=ω/ωn​=f/fn​ (dimensionless; rad/s ÷ rad/s — checks out). Divide the numerator and denominator of the canonical Section-10.2 ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 by ωn4\omega_n^4ωn4​:

∣Hlp∣2=(2ζωnω)2+ωn4(ωn2−ω2)2+(2ζωnω)2=1+4ζ2x2(1−x2)2+4ζ2x2≡g(x).\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2=\frac{(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2+\omega_n^4}{(\omega_n^2-\omega^2)^2+(2\zeta\omega_n\omega)^2} =\frac{1+4\zeta^2x^2}{(1-x^2)^2+4\zeta^2x^2}\equiv g(x) .∣Hlp​∣2=(ωn2​−ω2)2+(2ζωn​ω)2(2ζωn​ω)2+ωn4​​=(1−x2)2+4ζ2x21+4ζ2x2​≡g(x).

Finding the extremum: a beautiful quadratic​

Let u=x2u=x^2u=x2 (u≥0u\ge0u≥0). Numerator N(u)=1+4ζ2uN(u)=1+4\zeta^2uN(u)=1+4ζ2u, denominator D(u)=(1−u)2+4ζ2u=u2+(4ζ2−2)u+1D(u)=(1-u)^2+4\zeta^2u=u^2+(4\zeta^2-2)u+1D(u)=(1−u)2+4ζ2u=u2+(4ζ2−2)u+1, derivatives N′=4ζ2N'=4\zeta^2N′=4ζ2, D′=2u+4ζ2−2D'=2u+4\zeta^2-2D′=2u+4ζ2−2. The extremum condition of the quotient is N′D−ND′=0N'D-ND'=0N′D−ND′=0; expand term by term:

N′D−ND′=4ζ2[u2+(4ζ2−2)u+1]−(1+4ζ2u)[2u+4ζ2−2]=[4ζ2u2+(16ζ4−8ζ2)u+4ζ2]−[8ζ2u2+(16ζ4−8ζ2)u+2u+4ζ2−2]=−4ζ2u2−2u+2  =  −2(2ζ2u2+u−1).\begin{aligned} N'D-ND'&=4\zeta^2\big[u^2+(4\zeta^2-2)u+1\big]-(1+4\zeta^2u)\big[2u+4\zeta^2-2\big]\\ &=\big[4\zeta^2u^2+(16\zeta^4-8\zeta^2)u+4\zeta^2\big]-\big[8\zeta^2u^2+(16\zeta^4-8\zeta^2)u+2u+4\zeta^2-2\big]\\ &=-4\zeta^2u^2-2u+2\;=\;-2\big(2\zeta^2u^2+u-1\big). \end{aligned}N′D−ND′​=4ζ2[u2+(4ζ2−2)u+1]−(1+4ζ2u)[2u+4ζ2−2]=[4ζ2u2+(16ζ4−8ζ2)u+4ζ2]−[8ζ2u2+(16ζ4−8ζ2)u+2u+4ζ2−2]=−4ζ2u2−2u+2=−2(2ζ2u2+u−1).​

(The two 16ζ416\zeta^416ζ4 cross terms cancel exactly, leaving a quadratic with no ζ4\zeta^4ζ4.) Setting it to zero and taking the positive root:

2ζ2u2+u−1=0⟹u\*=1+8ζ2−14ζ2=21+8ζ2+1,fpk=fnu\*.2\zeta^2u^2+u-1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u^\*=\frac{\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}-1}{4\zeta^2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}+1},\qquad f_{pk}=f_n\sqrt{u^\*}.2ζ2u2+u−1=0⟹u\*=4ζ21+8ζ2​−1​=1+8ζ2​+12​,fpk​=fn​u\*​.

(The two forms are equal: multiply numerator and denominator by 1+8ζ2+1\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}+11+8ζ2​+1 and use 8ζ2=(1+8ζ2)2−18\zeta^2=(\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2})^2-18ζ2=(1+8ζ2​)2−1.)

Why it "always" peaks​

At u=0u=0u=0 (DC), N′D−ND′=4ζ2−(4ζ2−2)=+2N'D-ND'=4\zeta^2-(4\zeta^2-2)=+2N′D−ND′=4ζ2−(4ζ2−2)=+2 — positive for every ζ\zetaζ. The DC gain is 1 and the slope points up, so for any finite ζ\zetaζ, u\*>0u^\*>0u\*>0 always holds and the peak is necessarily above 0 dB. The physical reason: a type-II loop has two integrators (open-loop phase starts at −180∘-180^\circ−180∘) and can only be stabilized by the loop filter's zero (fz=fn/(2ζ)f_z=f_n/(2\zeta)fz​=fn​/(2ζ)) pulling the phase back early; that zero first lifts the closed-loop gain above 1 before the double pole pushes it down — peaking is the price of type-II stability, not a design mistake. Contrast: an ordinary second-order low-pass without a zero has no resonance peak for ζ≥1/2\zeta\ge1/\sqrt2ζ≥1/2​; a type-II with a zero always peaks, the peak merely getting lower and sliding toward lower frequency as ζ\zetaζ grows.

Peak magnitude: substitute back and simplify​

Let s=1+8ζ2s=\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}s=1+8ζ2​ (dimensionless). Three intermediate quantities, simplified step by step (using 8ζ2=s2−18\zeta^2=s^2-18ζ2=s2−1 repeatedly):

N(u\*)=1+4ζ2u\*=1+(s−1)=s,1−u\*=1−2s+1=s−1s+1,D(u\*)=(s−1s+1)2+(s−1)=(s−1)[(s−1)+(s+1)2](s+1)2=s (s−1)(s+3)(s+1)2.\begin{aligned} N(u^\*)&=1+4\zeta^2u^\*=1+(s-1)=s,\\ 1-u^\*&=1-\frac{2}{s+1}=\frac{s-1}{s+1},\\ D(u^\*)&=\Big(\frac{s-1}{s+1}\Big)^2+(s-1) =\frac{(s-1)\big[(s-1)+(s+1)^2\big]}{(s+1)^2} =\frac{s\,(s-1)(s+3)}{(s+1)^2}. \end{aligned}N(u\*)1−u\*D(u\*)​=1+4ζ2u\*=1+(s−1)=s,=1−s+12​=s+1s−1​,=(s+1s−1​)2+(s−1)=(s+1)2(s−1)[(s−1)+(s+1)2]​=(s+1)2s(s−1)(s+3)​.​

(The last step uses (s−1)+(s+1)2=s2+3s=s(s+3)(s-1)+(s+1)^2=s^2+3s=s(s+3)(s−1)+(s+1)2=s2+3s=s(s+3).) Therefore

∣Hlp∣max2=N(u\*)D(u\*)=(s+1)2(s−1)(s+3),fpk=fn2s+1,s=1+8ζ2.\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2_{max}=\frac{N(u^\*)}{D(u^\*)}=\frac{(s+1)^2}{(s-1)(s+3)},\qquad f_{pk}=f_n\sqrt{\frac{2}{s+1}},\qquad s=\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}.∣Hlp​∣max2​=D(u\*)N(u\*)​=(s−1)(s+3)(s+1)2​,fpk​=fn​s+12​​,s=1+8ζ2​.

Peaking (dB) =10log⁡10∣Hlp∣max2=10\log_{10}\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2_{max}=10log10​∣Hlp​∣max2​. dB bookkeeping note: this is 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ of a power transfer, numerically equal to 20log⁡1020\log_{10}20log10​ of the magnitude transfer — the same number; there is no SSB /2 or /4 bookkeeping here (that only arises when converting SϕS_\phiSϕ​ to L\mathcal{L}L — see canonical Eq. 16 and the [P1] Eq.(21) discussion).

Dimension check: x,u,ζ,sx,u,\zeta,sx,u,ζ,s are all dimensionless; fpk=fn×f_{pk}=f_n\timesfpk​=fn​×(dimensionless) === Hz — checks out; ∣Hlp∣max2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2_{max}∣Hlp​∣max2​ is a dimensionless power ratio — checks out.

The +1.76+1.76+1.76 dB read at fnf_nfn​ in Step 3 is only the right shoulder of this peak.

Where the ζ↔\zeta\leftrightarrowζ↔PM mapping comes from: back out the open loop from HlpH_{lp}Hlp​, G(s)=Hlp/(1−Hlp)=(2ζωns+ωn2)/s2G(s)=H_{lp}/(1-H_{lp})=(2\zeta\omega_n s+\omega_n^2)/s^2G(s)=Hlp​/(1−Hlp​)=(2ζωn​s+ωn2​)/s2; setting ∣G(jωc)∣=1\lvert G(j\omega_c)\rvert=1∣G(jωc​)∣=1 gives the crossover frequency ωc=ωn2ζ2+4ζ4+1\omega_c=\omega_n\sqrt{2\zeta^2+\sqrt{4\zeta^4+1}}ωc​=ωn​2ζ2+4ζ4+1​​; and ∠G=−180∘+arctan⁡(2ζωc/ωn)\angle G=-180^\circ+\arctan(2\zeta\omega_c/\omega_n)∠G=−180∘+arctan(2ζωc​/ωn​), hence

PM=arctan⁡ ⁣(2ζ2ζ2+4ζ4+1).\mathrm{PM}=\arctan\!\Big(2\zeta\sqrt{2\zeta^2+\sqrt{4\zeta^4+1}}\Big).PM=arctan(2ζ2ζ2+4ζ4+1​​).

This expression is identical in form to the textbook "standard second-order system (no-zero prototype)" ζ↔\zeta\leftrightarrowζ↔PM mapping (the algebraic identity (4ζ4+1−2ζ2)(4ζ4+1+2ζ2)=1(\sqrt{4\zeta^4+1}-2\zeta^2)(\sqrt{4\zeta^4+1}+2\zeta^2)=1(4ζ4+1​−2ζ2)(4ζ4+1​+2ζ2)=1 makes the two arctan⁡\arctanarctan arguments equal), so the common rule of thumb PM≈100 ζ\mathrm{PM}\approx100\,\zetaPM≈100ζ degrees (valid for ζ≲0.7\zeta\lesssim0.7ζ≲0.7) carries over as well (the standard ζ↔\zeta\leftrightarrowζ↔PM mapping and the 100ζ100\zeta100ζ rule are external literature, not among this site's five source PDFs: F. M. Gardner, Phaselock Techniques, 3rd ed., Wiley, 2005; B. Razavi, Design of CMOS Phase-Locked Loops, Cambridge Univ. Press, 2020).

The cascade rule: why telecom specs obsess over 0.1 dB​

Cascade MMM loops with identical transfers (a chain of repeaters/CDRs on a long-haul link, each regenerating and re-transmitting the clock): the total jitter transfer is HlpMH_{lp}^MHlpM​ — the dBs add directly: the peak becomes M×PM\times PM×P dB.

  • 2.09 dB per stage (ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707) ×\times× 20 stages === 41.8 dB: jitter near fpkf_{pk}fpk​ is amplified more than a hundredfold — the link is dead.
  • 0.1 dB per stage ×\times× 20 stages === 2 dB: manageable.

This is why the SONET/SDH era pinned the regenerator jitter-transfer peaking spec at the 0.1 dB level (external standards literature: Telcordia GR-253-CORE and the ITU-T G.783/G.958 family of telecom specs; this site has not verified the individual clause numbers — we cite the magnitude and the spirit). Inverting the closed form, 0.1 dB requires ζ≈4.32\zeta\approx4.32ζ≈4.32 (PM ≈89.2∘\approx89.2^\circ≈89.2∘, heavily overdamped) — completely different from the ζ≈0.7\zeta\approx0.7ζ≈0.7–111 that minimizes a single PLL's integrated jitter: single-loop optimal is not cascade optimal; a CDR's ζ\zetaζ is a system spec set by "which stage of the chain you are."

Rigor note: adding dBs assumes every stage has the same fn,ζf_n,\zetafn​,ζ (peaks aligned — worst case); in practice the stages' fnf_nfn​ are slightly staggered and the compounding is milder than M×PM\times PM×P, but specs are written for the worst case.

Numerical cross-check (repo pll_utils)​

Closed form vs H_lowpass_mag2 from simulations/common/pll_utils.py (a 4-million-point fine sweep):

import numpy as np
from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2

def peak_closed(zeta):                      # closed form: f_pk/f_n and |H_lp|^2_max
    s = np.sqrt(1 + 8*zeta**2)
    return np.sqrt((s - 1)/(4*zeta**2)), (s + 1)**2/((s - 1)*(s + 3))

x = np.linspace(0.001, 5, 4_000_001)        # x = f/f_n (take f_n = 1 Hz)
for z in (0.5, 0.707, 1.0, 1.5):
    xpk, g = peak_closed(z)
    m2 = H_lowpass_mag2(x, 1.0, z)
    k = int(np.argmax(m2))
    print(f"{z}: closed {xpk:.4f}/{10*np.log10(g):.4f} dB, "
          f"numeric {x[k]:.4f}/{10*np.log10(m2[k]):.4f} dB")
# -> 0.707: closed 0.7862/2.0903 dB, numeric 0.7862/2.0903 dB (others: zeta=0.5→3.3339, 1.0→1.2494, 1.5→0.6514; closed = numeric to 4 decimals)

zg = np.linspace(2, 8, 600001)              # sweep zeta to invert for 0.1 dB peaking
pk = 10*np.log10(peak_closed(zg)[1])
z01 = zg[int(np.argmin(np.abs(pk - 0.1)))]
print(round(z01, 3))                        # -> 4.319 (zeta required for 0.1 dB)

Conditions of validity and failure (this section's closed form):

  • Valid only for the ideal type-II second-order closed loop of canonical Section 10.2 (linearized charge-pump PLL, no extra poles). Real loops usually add 1–2 high-frequency poles in the loop filter (third/fourth-order loops); the peak location and height shift and must be computed numerically.
  • The PM mapping assumes the crossover happens on the ideal G(s)G(s)G(s); extra poles eat PM, and PM≈100ζ\mathrm{PM}\approx100\zetaPM≈100ζ loses accuracy accordingly.
  • This peak is a bump of the transfer function; the actual PN bump near fnf_nfn​ at the output must still be multiplied by each source's PSD (see Step 3).

Step 4: reference spur (brief)​

Besides random phase noise (a continuous skirt), PLL output also commonly has discrete spurs (single-frequency spikes). The most common is the reference spur: the charge-pump injects a current pulse every reference period, and this periodic disturbance appears at the output at integer multiples of freff_{ref}fref​ (i.e. offset =±fref,±2fref,…=\pm f_{ref},\pm2f_{ref},\dots=±fref​,±2fref​,…). Its source is CP current mismatch, leakage, and PFD dead-zone, which impose a small freff_{ref}fref​ ripple on the control voltage, converted by the VCO's KvK_vKv​ into phase-modulation sidebands.

  • Spur vs. random PN: a spur is a deterministic, narrow line (a needle in the spectrum), random PN is a continuous skirt; in measurement, the spur's height doesn't change with resolution bandwidth RBW (its power is concentrated in one bin), whereas random PN's dBc/Hz is genuinely "per-Hz."
  • Relation to loop BW: the reference spur at offset freff_{ref}fref​, if fref>fnf_{ref}>f_nfref​>fn​, is attenuated by ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2's low-pass (narrower loop BW → more spur suppression); this is consistent with "narrow BW favors random in-band noise," but it sacrifices VCO suppression — the same trade-off again.
  • This page's budget only covers the random part (continuous SoutS_{out}Sout​); a quantitative spur analysis belongs to standard PLL literature (not among the five source PDFs) — here it's only a conceptual link.

Step 5: optimal loop BW — minimizing ∫S_out df​

Write out the output's integrated phase variance (canonical Eq. 18):

σϕ2(fn)=∫f1f2Sout(f;fn) df,σt(fn)=12πf0σϕ2(fn).\sigma_\phi^2(f_n)=\int_{f_1}^{f_2}S_{out}(f;f_n)\,df,\qquad \sigma_t(f_n)=\frac{1}{2\pi f_0}\sqrt{\sigma_\phi^2(f_n)} .σϕ2​(fn​)=∫f1​f2​​Sout​(f;fn​)df,σt​(fn​)=2πf0​1​σϕ2​(fn​)​.

σϕ2\sigma_\phi^2σϕ2​ is a function of fnf_nfn​, because SoutS_{out}Sout​ depends on fnf_nfn​ through ∣Hlp∣2,∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2,\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2,∣Hhp​∣2. Split it into in-band and out-of-band pieces to see the trend:

σϕ2(fn)≈∫(SrefN2+Scp) ∣Hlp∣2 df⏟↑ as fn↑ (wider passband, more ref/CP carried through)+∫Svco ∣Hhp∣2 df⏟↓ as fn↑ (more VCO close-in suppressed).\sigma_\phi^2(f_n)\approx\underbrace{\int (S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\,df}_{\uparrow\ \text{as }f_n\uparrow\ (\text{wider passband, more ref/CP carried through})}+\underbrace{\int S_{vco}\,\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\,df}_{\downarrow\ \text{as }f_n\uparrow\ (\text{more VCO close-in suppressed})} .σϕ2​(fn​)≈↑ as fn​↑ (wider passband, more ref/CP carried through)∫(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2df​​+↓ as fn​↑ (more VCO close-in suppressed)∫Svco​∣Hhp​∣2df​​.
  • First term (ref/CP) increases monotonically with fnf_nfn​: the larger fnf_nfn​, the wider the low-pass passband, carrying more of the in-band floor (including the N2N^2N2-amplified reference) through to the output. Roughly ∝(SrefN2+Scp)⋅fn\propto(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\cdot f_n∝(Sref​N2+Scp​)⋅fn​ (flat floor times passband width).
  • Second term (VCO) decreases monotonically with fnf_nfn​: the larger fnf_nfn​, the more of the VCO's 1/f21/f^21/f2 close-in the high-pass corrects away. For Svco=k/f2S_{vco}=k/f^2Svco​=k/f2 passed through the high-pass, the residual integral ∝k/fn\propto k/f_n∝k/fn​ (wider BW → less leakage).

One increasing, one decreasing → a U-shape. Setting the derivative with respect to fnf_nfn​ to zero gives a unique minimum:

d σϕ2dfn=0⟹(marginal increase in ref/CP leakage)=(marginal decrease in VCO suppression).\frac{d\,\sigma_\phi^2}{d f_n}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{(marginal increase in ref/CP leakage)}=\text{(marginal decrease in VCO suppression)}.dfn​dσϕ2​​=0␀⟹(marginal increase in ref/CP leakage)=(marginal decrease in VCO suppression).

Using the two rough estimates above (of the form a fn+b/fna\,f_n+b/f_nafn​+b/fn​, with a∝SrefN2+Scpa\propto S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}a∝Sref​N2+Scp​ and b∝Svcob\propto S_{vco}b∝Svco​'s coefficient) to find the minimum:

ddfn ⁣(afn+bfn)=a−bfn2=0 ⟹ fn\*=ba ∝ Svco coefficientSrefN2+Scp.\frac{d}{df_n}\!\left(a f_n+\frac{b}{f_n}\right)=a-\frac{b}{f_n^2}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ f_n^\*=\sqrt{\frac{b}{a}}\ \propto\ \sqrt{\frac{S_{vco}\text{ coefficient}}{S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}}} .dfn​d​(afn​+fn​b​)=a−fn2​b​=0 ⟹ fn\*​=ab​​ ∝ Sref​N2+Scp​Svco​ coefficient​​.
  • Physical meaning: the noisier the VCO (bbb large) → the larger the optimal BW (a wider loop is needed to suppress the VCO); the noisier the ref/CP, or the larger NNN (aaa large) → the smaller the optimal BW (you can't afford to carry too much of the in-band floor through). This relation fn\*∝b/af_n^\*\propto\sqrt{b/a}fn\*​∝b/a​ is the core intuition of PLL design, though the coefficients must be pinned down by numerical integration.
  • Toy-model note: the afn+b/fnaf_n+b/f_nafn​+b/fn​ above is a heuristic estimate that approximates the shaping as an ideal brick-wall filter; the real integral needs the full ∣H∣2\lvert H\rvert^2∣H∣2 (including the peaking near fnf_nfn​), so below we use lab_20's numerical integration to give the exact minimum.

The minimum lands at fn\*≈6.90f_n^\*\approx6.90fn\*​≈6.90 MHz, σt≈259\sigma_t\approx259σt​≈259 fs (lab_20's measured printed values).

Core Python (full script: simulations/lab_20_pll_budget.py):

import numpy as np
from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2, H_highpass_mag2

def output_psd(f, fn, N, zeta=0.707):
    lp = H_lowpass_mag2(f, fn, zeta)
    hp = H_highpass_mag2(f, fn, zeta)
    S_ref = 1e-16 + 1e-18 * (1e6 / f)   # clean crystal
    S_cp  = 5e-13 * np.ones_like(f)     # PFD/CP/divider flat floor
    S_vco = 2e-10 * (1e6 / f) ** 2      # ring VCO -100 dBc/Hz @1MHz, 1/f^2
    return (S_ref * N**2 + S_cp) * lp + S_vco * hp   # budget sum

f = np.logspace(3, 9, 3000); f0 = 5e9; N = 100
fns = np.logspace(4.5, 7.5, 60)
jit = [np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(output_psd(f, fn, N), f)) / (2*np.pi*f0) for fn in fns]
k = int(np.argmin(jit))
print(fns[k]/1e6, "MHz", jit[k]*1e15, "fs")   # -> ~6.90 MHz, ~259 fs

Worked examples​

Format: problem → step-by-step substitution (with units) → result → dimension check → one line of Python verification. Uses lab_20's representative values throughout (f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz, N=100N=100N=100, ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707, the three SSS's from the table above).

Example 1 (in-band floor + the cost of the reference's ×N2\times N^2×N2): find the deep in-band (f≪fnf\ll f_nf≪fn​) output phase-noise floor, convert it to dBc/Hz, and compare how much difference (in dB) it makes if NNN drops from 100 to 10.

Step by step:

  1. Deep in-band, ∣Hlp∣2≈1\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1∣Hlp​∣2≈1, ∣Hhp∣2≈0\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2\approx0∣Hhp​∣2≈0; take the flat part (ignoring the reference's 1/f1/f1/f):
Sout, in-band≈SrefN2+Scp=10−16×1002+5×10−13.S_{out,\,\text{in-band}}\approx S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}=10^{-16}\times100^2+5\times10^{-13}.Sout,in-band​≈Sref​N2+Scp​=10−16×1002+5×10−13.
  1. Compute the reference term: 10−16×104=10−12 rad2/Hz10^{-16}\times10^{4}=10^{-12}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}10−16×104=10−12 rad2/Hz.
  2. Add the CP term: 10−12+5×10−13=1.5×10−12 rad2/Hz10^{-12}+5\times10^{-13}=1.5\times10^{-12}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}10−12+5×10−13=1.5×10−12 rad2/Hz.
  3. Convert to dBc/Hz (L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12 S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​, canonical Eq. 16): L=10log⁡10(12×1.5×10−12)=10log⁡10(7.5×10−13)\mathcal{L}=10\log_{10}(\tfrac12\times1.5\times10^{-12})=10\log_{10}(7.5\times10^{-13})L=10log10​(21​×1.5×10−12)=10log10​(7.5×10−13).

Result: the in-band floor Sout≈1.5×10−12 rad2/HzS_{out}\approx1.5\times10^{-12}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}Sout​≈1.5×10−12 rad2/Hz, i.e. L≈−121.2\mathcal{L}\approx-121.2L≈−121.2 dBc/Hz. Of this, the reference contributes 10−1210^{-12}10−12 and the CP contributes 0.5×10−120.5\times10^{-12}0.5×10−12 — the reference×N2\times N^2×N2 is the dominant player in-band. If NNN drops from 100 to 10, the reference term drops from 10−1210^{-12}10−12 to 10−16×100=10−1410^{-16}\times100=10^{-14}10−16×100=10−14 (a drop of 100×=20100\times=20100×=20 dB), and in-band is now dominated by Scp=5×10−13S_{cp}=5\times10^{-13}Scp​=5×10−13, with the total floor ≈5.1×10␀−13\approx5.1\times10^{-13}≈5.1×10−13 — an improvement of about 10log⁡10(1.5×10−12/5.1×10−13)≈4.710\log_{10}(1.5\times10^{-12}/5.1\times10^{-13})\approx4.710log10​(1.5×10−12/5.1×10−13)≈4.7 dB.

import numpy as np
S_ref, N, S_cp = 1e-16, 100, 5e-13
S_in = S_ref*N**2 + S_cp
print(S_in, "rad^2/Hz", round(10*np.log10(0.5*S_in), 1), "dBc/Hz")  # 1.5e-12, -121.2

Example 2 (the U-shape and optimal BW: narrow, optimal, wide — three points compared): using lab_20's complete budget, numerically integrate from 1 kHz–1 GHz, and compare the rms jitter at fn=0.3f_n=0.3fn​=0.3 MHz (too narrow), fn\*≈6.9f_n^\*\approx6.9fn\*​≈6.9 MHz (optimal), and fn=30f_n=30fn​=30 MHz (too wide), to verify the U-shape and its minimum.

Steps (concept + numerics):

  1. For each fnf_nfn​, compute Sout(f;fn)=(SrefN2+Scp)∣Hlp∣2+Svco∣Hhp∣2S_{out}(f;f_n)=(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+S_{vco}\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2Sout​(f;fn​)=(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2 frequency by frequency.
  2. Integrate to get σϕ2=∫103109Sout df\sigma_\phi^2=\int_{10^3}^{10^9}S_{out}\,dfσϕ2​=∫103109​Sout​df (trapezoid rule), then take the square root to get σϕ\sigma_\phiσϕ​.
  3. Convert to σt=σϕ/(2πf0)\sigma_t=\sigma_\phi/(2\pi f_0)σt​=σϕ​/(2πf0​), with f0=5f_0=5f0​=5 GHz.

Result (lab_20 numerics):

fnf_nfn​σt\sigma_tσt​What leaks through
0.30 MHz (too narrow)≈867\approx867≈867 fslarge VCO close-in leakage (U-shape's left arm)
6.90 MHz (optimal)≈259\approx259≈259 fsbalanced on both sides, the minimum
30 MHz (too wide)≈396\approx396≈396 fsref×N2\times N^2×N2/CP carried through (U-shape's right arm)

Moving from the optimum toward narrow (6.9→0.36.9\to0.36.9→0.3 MHz), jitter rises to 3.3×3.3\times3.3×; moving toward wide (6.9→306.9\to306.9→30 MHz), it rises to 1.5×1.5\times1.5×. The U-shape's left arm is steeper than the right — because this is a ring VCO (SvcoS_{vco}Svco​ large, its 1/f21/f^21/f2 leakage very sensitive to BW), so "better to open it a bit wide than too narrow." This is exactly the design rule behind ring-PLLs' preference for large loop BW.

Dimension check: ∫Sout df\int S_{out}\,df∫Sout​df: [rad2/Hz]×[Hz]=[rad2][\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]\times[\text{Hz}]=[\text{rad}^2][rad2/Hz]×[Hz]=[rad2] → σϕ [rad]\sigma_\phi\,[\text{rad}]σϕ​[rad]; σϕ/(2πf0)\sigma_\phi/(2\pi f_0)σϕ​/(2πf0​): rad/(rad/s)=s\text{rad}/(\text{rad/s})=\text{s}rad/(rad/s)=s — confirmed.

import numpy as np
from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2, H_highpass_mag2
f = np.logspace(3, 9, 3000); f0 = 5e9; N = 100
def Sout(fn):
    lp, hp = H_lowpass_mag2(f, fn), H_highpass_mag2(f, fn)
    S_ref = 1e-16 + 1e-18*(1e6/f); S_cp = 5e-13; S_vco = 2e-10*(1e6/f)**2
    return (S_ref*N**2 + S_cp)*lp + S_vco*hp
for fn in [0.3e6, 6.9e6, 30e6]:
    st = np.sqrt(np.trapezoid(Sout(fn), f))/(2*np.pi*f0)
    print(f"fn={fn/1e6:5.2f} MHz -> sigma_t={st*1e15:.0f} fs")  # 867 / 259 / 396 fs

The third term for fractional-N: ΔΣ quantization noise​

The budget so far is integer-N: fout=Nfreff_{out}=Nf_{ref}fout​=Nfref​, so the frequency step can only be an integer multiple of freff_{ref}fref​. For fine steps (e.g. a 200-kHz channel spacing) without sacrificing freff_{ref}fref​, you need fractional-N (fractional division): dither the modulus between integers (÷NNN this reference period, ÷(N+1)(N{+}1)(N+1) the next, …) so the average modulus is N+αN+\alphaN+α (0≤α<10\le\alpha<10≤α<1). This pays a double dividend — freff_{ref}fref​ can be raised and NNN shrinks, so the in-band SrefN2S_{ref}N^2Sref​N2 floor drops directly — but the modulus dithering is itself a quantization error and becomes a new noise source. Generating the modulus sequence with a ΔΣ modulator (delta-sigma modulator — a feedback quantizer that shapes the quantization error toward high frequencies) pushes the error power out to high offsets where the loop's low-pass filters it away. This section writes it up as the budget's third term.

The shaped result in this section belongs to standard ΔΣ frequency-synthesis theory (external literature, not among this site's five source PDFs); the classic source: T. A. D. Riley, M. A. Copeland, and T. A. Kwasniewski, "Delta-Sigma Modulation in Fractional-N Frequency Synthesis," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 28, no. 5, pp. 553–559, May 1993. The derivation below is self-contained, step by step.

From modulus dithering to phase noise (four steps)​

(i) The MASH-m output. An mmm-th-order MASH (MASH-1-1-1 means m=3m=3m=3: three cascaded first-order accumulators) produces the modulus-control sequence

y[k]=α+(1−z−1)m e[k],y[k]=\alpha+(1-z^{-1})^m\,e[k],y[k]=α+(1−z−1)me[k],

where e[k]e[k]e[k] is the last stage's quantization error, modeled as white: uniformly distributed over ±Δ/2\pm\Delta/2±Δ/2, variance σe2=Δ2/12\sigma_e^2=\Delta^2/12σe2​=Δ2/12, with Δ=1\Delta=1Δ=1 LSB (note: this Δ\DeltaΔ is the quantization step === 1 VCO cycle per reference period — not the Δ\DeltaΔ of the offset Δf\Delta fΔf). The (1−z−1)m(1-z^{-1})^m(1−z−1)m is the ΔΣ noise shaping: it pushes the error power toward high frequencies.

(ii) The error accumulates into phase (one integration). In reference period kkk the divider swallows y[k]−αy[k]-\alphay[k]−α extra VCO cycles; each cycle is 2π2\pi2π rad of output phase, and phase is the accumulation of frequency error:

ϕΔΣ[k]=2π∑j≤k(y[j]−α)=2π (1−z−1)m−1e[k][rad].\phi_{\Delta\Sigma}[k]=2\pi\sum_{j\le k}\big(y[j]-\alpha\big)=2\pi\,(1-z^{-1})^{m-1}e[k]\quad[\text{rad}] .ϕΔΣ​[k]=2πj≤k∑​(y[j]−α)=2π(1−z−1)m−1e[k][rad].

(Accumulation is 1/(1−z−1)1/(1-z^{-1})1/(1−z−1) in the zzz-domain, which eats exactly one order of shaping: mmm-th-order frequency shaping → (m−1)(m-1)(m−1)-th-order phase shaping.)

(iii) PSD of the white sequence. A white sequence at sampling rate freff_{ref}fref​ spreads its power σe2\sigma_e^2σe2​ uniformly over ±fref/2\pm f_{ref}/2±fref​/2 (two-sided bookkeeping) → density σe2/fref=Δ2/(12fref)\sigma_e^2/f_{ref}=\Delta^2/(12f_{ref})σe2​/fref​=Δ2/(12fref​) per Hz; the discrete difference has magnitude response ∣1−e−j2πf/fref∣=2∣sin⁡(πf/fref)∣\lvert1-e^{-j2\pi f/f_{ref}}\rvert=2\lvert\sin(\pi f/f_{ref})\rvert∣1−e−j2πf/fref​∣=2∣sin(πf/fref​)∣. Putting it together (referred to the output phase, before the loop):

LΔΣ(f)=(2πΔ)212 fref[2sin⁡(πffref)]2(m−1),SΔΣ(f)=2 LΔΣ(f)=(2πΔ)26 fref[2sin⁡(πffref)]2(m−1)\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)=\frac{(2\pi\Delta)^2}{12\,f_{ref}}\Big[2\sin\Big(\frac{\pi f}{f_{ref}}\Big)\Big]^{2(m-1)},\qquad S_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)=2\,\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)=\frac{(2\pi\Delta)^2}{6\,f_{ref}}\Big[2\sin\Big(\frac{\pi f}{f_{ref}}\Big)\Big]^{2(m-1)}LΔΣ​(f)=12fref​(2πΔ)2​[2sin(fref​πf​)]2(m−1),SΔΣ​(f)=2LΔΣ​(f)=6fref​(2πΔ)2​[2sin(fref​πf​)]2(m−1)

(SΔΣS_{\Delta\Sigma}SΔΣ​ in rad2/Hz\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}rad2/Hz, single-sided). Factor-of-2 bookkeeping flag (flagged every time): the literature's customary 1/121/121/12 version is two-sided bookkeeping, which numerically happens to equal the SSB L\mathcal{L}L (because the 12\tfrac1221​ in L≈12Sϕ\mathcal{L}\approx\tfrac12S_\phiL≈21​Sϕ​ cancels the ×2\times2×2 of single-siding); this site's strict single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​ convention needs the ×2\times2×2 (giving 1/61/61/6). Both notations appear in the literature — always state which one you are reading. This is the same class of factor-of-2 issue as [P1] Eq.(21)'s /4 (SSB bookkeeping) vs the clean time-domain /2.

(iv) No ×N2\times N^2×N2! This term enters the loop at the PFD like SrefS_{ref}Sref​ and is low-passed by the same ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2, but it is not multiplied by N2N^2N2: the error is counted in "VCO cycles" to begin with, so the 2π2\pi2π is already rad of output phase. If you insist on referring it to the divider output (only 2π/N2\pi/N2π/N rad per cycle), you must multiply by NNN (power ×N2\times N^2×N2) to get back to the output — the N2N^2N2 cancels exactly. The most common rookie budget mistake is multiplying this term by N2N^2N2 anyway.

Dimension check: (2πΔ)2(2\pi\Delta)^2(2πΔ)2 [rad²] (Δ\DeltaΔ is a dimensionless cycle count) ×\times× 1/(12fref)1/(12f_{ref})1/(12fref​) [1/Hz] ×\times× shaping factor [dimensionless] =rad2/Hz=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}=rad2/Hz — checks out.

Into the budget: the third term​

Sout(f)=(SrefN2+Scp)∣Hlp∣2+Svco∣Hhp∣2+SΔΣ(f) ∣Hlp∣2.S_{out}(f)=\big(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp}\big)\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+S_{vco}\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2+S_{\Delta\Sigma}(f)\,\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2 .Sout​(f)=(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2+SΔΣ​(f)∣Hlp​∣2.

It shares the CP noise's path (low-pass) but has a completely different shape: for f≪freff\ll f_{ref}f≪fref​, 2sin⁡(πf/fref)≈2πf/fref2\sin(\pi f/f_{ref})\approx2\pi f/f_{ref}2sin(πf/fref​)≈2πf/fref​, so

SΔΣ∝f 2(m−1)S_{\Delta\Sigma}\propto f^{\,2(m-1)}SΔΣ​∝f2(m−1)

— a rising ramp of 20(m−1)20(m-1)20(m−1) dB/dec (MASH-1-1-1: +40+40+40 dB/dec), capping out at fref/2f_{ref}/2fref​/2 (shaping factor at most 22(m−1)=162^{2(m-1)}=1622(m−1)=16, i.e. +12.0+12.0+12.0 dB). It is not a floor — it is a wall climbing up from low frequency; the loop must chop it with ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 before the wall climbs high enough to hurt.

The two suppression knobs (why higher freff_{ref}fref​ and narrower BW work):

  • Raise freff_{ref}fref​: at fixed f≪freff\ll f_{ref}f≪fref​, LΔΣ∝f2(m−1)/fref 2m−1\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}\propto f^{2(m-1)}/f_{ref}^{\,2m-1}LΔΣ​∝f2(m−1)/fref2m−1​ — doubling freff_{ref}fref​ drops it by (2m−1)×3.01≈15.05(2m-1)\times3.01\approx15.05(2m−1)×3.01≈15.05 dB (m=3m=3m=3). Intuition: the total quantization power Δ2/12\Delta^2/12Δ2/12 is fixed but spread over a wider Nyquist bandwidth, and the freff_{ref}fref​ in the shaping denominator grows.
  • Narrow the loop BW: the in-band spot value doesn't change (∣Hlp∣2≈1\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2\approx1∣Hlp​∣2≈1), but the low-pass intercepts the ramp earlier — the third term's peak lands near ∼fn\sim f_n∼fn​ with magnitude ∝fn2(m−1)\propto f_n^{2(m-1)}∝fn2(m−1)​ (m=3m=3m=3: halving fnf_nfn​ drops the peak 12 dB); a brick-wall estimate of its integrated power scales as ∝fn2m−1\propto f_n^{2m-1}∝fn2m−1​ (fn5f_n^5fn5​ — extremely sensitive to BW). This pushes in the same direction as the U-shape's right arm ("narrow BW suppresses in-band"), but directly conflicts with a ring VCO's need for wide BW — fractional-N + a noisy VCO is the hardest budget combination, and one reason low-noise fractional-N synthesizers prefer LC VCOs.

Honest toy-model warning (important): this page's type-II second-order ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 only falls −20-20−20 dB/dec beyond fnf_nfn​ — it cannot catch the +40+40+40 dB/dec rise of m=3m=3m=3. So in this toy model the third term keeps climbing at a net +20+20+20 dB/dec past fnf_nfn​ until the sin⁡\sinsin caps: with fn=100f_n=100fn​=100 kHz the peak is −103.6-103.6−103.6 dBc/Hz at ≈18.6\approx18.6≈18.6 MHz, about 22 dB above the VCO term at the same offset (−125.4-125.4−125.4 dBc/Hz). Real fractional-N loops therefore must add high-frequency loop-filter poles (third/ fourth-order loops) so the out-of-band rolloff beats 20(m−1)20(m-1)20(m−1) dB/dec (external standard practice — see the Gardner and Razavi textbooks; not among this site's five source PDFs). This is the classic origin of "the third term looks harmless on paper, then a high-frequency hump pops up in silicon."

Worked example (Example 3: the MASH-1-1-1 spot contribution)​

Example 3: MASH-1-1-1 (m=3m=3m=3), fref=50f_{ref}=50fref​=50 MHz, Δ=1\Delta=1Δ=1, ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707. Find LΔΣ\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}LΔΣ​ at f=1f=1f=1 MHz (first without the loop, then through ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 with fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz and 100 kHz respectively), and compare against this page's in-band floor of −121.2-121.2−121.2 dBc/Hz.

Step by step:

  1. Prefactor: (2π×1)212×50×106=39.4786×108=6.580×10−8 rad2/Hz\dfrac{(2\pi\times1)^2}{12\times50\times10^6}=\dfrac{39.478}{6\times10^8}=6.580\times10^{-8}\ \text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}12×50×106(2π×1)2​=6×10839.478​=6.580×10−8 rad2/Hz.
  2. Shaping factor: 2sin⁡(π×106/(5×107))=2sin⁡(0.06283 rad)=0.125582\sin\big(\pi\times10^6/(5\times10^7)\big)=2\sin(0.06283\ \text{rad})=0.125582sin(π×106/(5×107))=2sin(0.06283 rad)=0.12558; raised to the 2(m−1)=42(m-1)=42(m−1)=4 → 2.487×10−42.487\times10^{-4}2.487×10−4 (dimensionless).
  3. Before the loop: 6.580×10−8×2.487×10−4=1.636×10−116.580\times10^{-8}\times2.487\times10^{-4}=1.636\times10^{-11}6.580×10−8×2.487×10−4=1.636×10−11 → LΔΣ(1 MHz)=−107.9\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}(1\text{ MHz})=-107.9LΔΣ​(1 MHz)=−107.9 dBc/Hz.
  4. fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz: ∣Hlp(1 MHz)∣2=1.50\lvert H_{lp}(1\text{ MHz})\rvert^2=1.50∣Hlp​(1 MHz)∣2=1.50 (+1.76+1.76+1.76 dB) → −106.1-106.1−106.1 dBc/Hz — 15 dB above the −121.2-121.2−121.2 dBc/Hz floor; the in-band budget is wrecked: the BW is too wide, the ramp has already climbed to its top at 1 MHz and gets a boost from the peaking.
  5. fn=100f_n=100fn​=100 kHz: ∣Hlp∣2=0.0201\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2=0.0201∣Hlp​∣2=0.0201 (−17.0-17.0−17.0 dB) → −124.8-124.8−124.8 dBc/Hz — pushed 3.6 dB below the floor, safe on a spot basis (but the high-frequency hump still needs checking — see the toy-model warning above).
  6. Alternatively, leave the BW alone and raise freff_{ref}fref​ to 100 MHz: before the loop it becomes −122.9-122.9−122.9 dBc/Hz, a 15.04-dB improvement (theoretical asymptote 15.0515.0515.05 dB — checks out).

Dimension check: rad2/Hz×\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}\timesrad2/Hz× dimensionless =rad2/Hz=\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}=rad2/Hz; after 10log⁡1010\log_{10}10log10​ it reads as dBc/Hz — checks out.

import numpy as np
from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_lowpass_mag2

fref, m, Delta, f = 50e6, 3, 1.0, 1e6
P = (2*np.pi*Delta)**2/(12*fref)
shape = (2*np.sin(np.pi*f/fref))**(2*(m - 1))
raw = P*shape
print(f"{P:.4e}", f"{shape:.4e}", round(10*np.log10(raw), 2))
# -> 6.5797e-08 2.4871e-04 -107.86 (prefactor rad^2/Hz, shaping factor, before-loop dBc/Hz)
for fn in (1e6, 1e5):
    lp = H_lowpass_mag2(np.array([f]), fn, 0.707)[0]
    print(round(fn/1e3), round(10*np.log10(raw*lp), 2))
# -> 1000 -106.1, 100 -124.83 (L_dSigma(1 MHz) for fn=1 MHz vs 100 kHz, dBc/Hz)
raw2 = (2*np.pi*Delta)**2/(12*100e6)*(2*np.sin(np.pi*f/100e6))**(2*(m - 1))
print(round(10*np.log10(raw/raw2), 2))
# -> 15.04 (improvement in dB for f_ref 50→100 MHz; asymptote (2m-1)x3.01=15.05)

fs = np.logspace(3, np.log10(25e6), 200_000)
LdS = P*(2*np.sin(np.pi*fs/fref))**(2*(m - 1))*H_lowpass_mag2(fs, 1e5, 0.707)
k = int(np.argmax(LdS))
print(round(10*np.log10(LdS[k]), 2), round(fs[k]/1e6, 2))
# -> -103.6 18.55 (the third term's high-frequency hump under the toy 2nd-order loop: dBc/Hz, MHz)

Conditions of validity and failure (the ΔΣ white-noise model)​

e[k]e[k]e[k] white, uniformα\alphaα is "busy" (no short limit cycle) or ditheredα\alphaα a simple fraction (e.g. 1/81/81/8) → periodic pattern → fractional spurs (discrete spikes, not a continuous spectrum)

Connection to SerDes​

The PLL output's σt\sigma_tσt​ (this page's right-panel minimum, ≈259\approx259≈259 fs) is exactly the jitter budget fed to a high-speed serializer/deserializer (SerDes)'s sampling clock. In serdes_clocking_connection, this σt\sigma_tσt​ directly determines the eye diagram's horizontal closure and BER (bit error rate): the shorter the UI (unit interval, i.e. the higher the data rate), the larger the fraction of the eye width the same σt\sigma_tσt​ eats up. So choosing the right loop BW to minimize PLL jitter is the source of the entire SerDes link's budget. The CDR (clock-data recovery) itself is also a PLL, and its jitter-tolerance transfer for input jitter is exactly this page's ∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2 (low-frequency jitter can be tracked → tolerated, high-frequency → relies on eye margin), see lab_13_pll_cdr_transfer.

Conditions of validity and failure​

ConditionHolds whenFails when
sources uncorrelatedpowers add directly (this page's sum formula)if CP and divider are correlated, cross terms are needed
linear PLL (small phase error)type-II second-order closed loop is validlarge unlock/slew → nonlinear, transfer function no longer holds
VCO is 1/f21/f^21/f2 (white-noise upconversion)Svco=k/f2S_{vco}=k/f^2Svco​=k/f2, this page's U-shapewith flicker (1/f31/f^31/f3 close-in) present → optimal BW shifts, re-integration needed
ignoring loop-filter and spurtoy budget is adequateprecise design must include SlfS_{lf}Slf​, reference spur, fractional spurs
integer-Nreference ×N2\times N^2×N2fractional-N: ΔΣ quantization-noise third term (now covered in this page's "The third term for fractional-N" section)

Key takeaways​

  • PLL output budget: Sout=(SrefN2+Scp)∣Hlp∣2+Svco∣Hhp∣2S_{out}=(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2+S_{vco}\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2Sout​=(Sref​N2+Scp​)∣Hlp​∣2+Svco​∣Hhp​∣2 (canonical 11.2).
  • In-band tracks ref/CP (amplified by N2N^2N2, low-passed), out-of-band tracks VCO (high-passed, 1/f21/f^21/f2 leakage), with the crossover at fnf_nfn​.
  • The VCO term is exactly this site's ISF result Svco∝Γrms2/qmax2⋅Si/f2S_{vco}\propto\Gamma_{rms}^2/q_{max}^2\cdot S_i/f^2Svco​∝Γrms2​/qmax2​⋅Si​/f2.
  • The reference spur is a discrete spike (the freff_{ref}fref​ ripple from CP mismatch/leakage), suppressed by a narrow BW but at the cost of VCO suppression.
  • Optimal loop BW: minimize ∫Soutdf\int S_{out}df∫Sout​df, fn\*∝Svco/(SrefN2+Scp)f_n^\*\propto\sqrt{S_{vco}/(S_{ref}N^2+S_{cp})}fn\*​∝Svco​/(Sref​N2+Scp​)​; too narrow leaks VCO, too wide leaks ref/CP. lab_20 numerics: fn\*≈6.90f_n^\*\approx6.90fn\*​≈6.90 MHz, σt≈259\sigma_t\approx259σt​≈259 fs.
  • This ring-PLL's U-shape has a steeper left arm than right → favors a somewhat larger loop BW.
  • A type-II with a zero always peaks: fpk=fn2/(s+1)f_{pk}=f_n\sqrt{2/(s+1)}fpk​=fn​2/(s+1)​, ∣Hlp∣max2=(s+1)2/[(s−1)(s+3)]\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2_{max}=(s+1)^2/[(s-1)(s+3)]∣Hlp​∣max2​=(s+1)2/[(s−1)(s+3)], s=1+8ζ2s=\sqrt{1+8\zeta^2}s=1+8ζ2​; ζ=0.707→2.09\zeta=0.707\to2.09ζ=0.707→2.09 dB @ 0.786fn0.786f_n0.786fn​ (the peak is exactly the golden ratio φ\varphiφ). In a cascade the peak dBs add → the 0.1-dB telecom spec (needs ζ≈4.3\zeta\approx4.3ζ≈4.3): single-loop optimal ≠\ne= cascade optimal.
  • The fractional-N third term: LΔΣ=(2πΔ)212fref[2sin⁡(πf/fref)]2(m−1)∣Hlp∣2\mathcal{L}_{\Delta\Sigma}=\frac{(2\pi\Delta)^2}{12f_{ref}}[2\sin(\pi f/f_{ref})]^{2(m-1)}\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2LΔΣ​=12fref​(2πΔ)2​[2sin(πf/fref​)]2(m−1)∣Hlp​∣2 (SSB reading; this site's single-sided SϕS_\phiSϕ​ needs ×2\times2×2), no ×N2\times N^2×N2, climbing at +40+40+40 dB/dec (m=3m=3m=3); doubling freff_{ref}fref​ gives −15-15−15 dB, a narrow BW chops the ramp; a 2nd-order loop cannot contain the m=3m=3m=3 high-frequency hump (add filter poles).
